families.name: Amplitude estimation (quantum Monte Carlo)
families.idea: Estimates an expectation with error falling as 1/N instead of 1/sqrt(N): a quadratic speed-up in the number of samples.
families.status: Speed-up proven in theory. Resource estimates for an autocall or TARF with advantage: about 7,500 logical qubits and a T-depth around 50 million, run in about a second (Chakrabarti et al., 2021). Loading distributions and payoffs into circuits dominates the cost. Only toy demonstrations so far.
families.noRegret: Variance reduction, quasi-Monte Carlo, AAD Greeks and GPU Monte Carlo. They set the bar any quantum pricer must beat, and they pay off now.

families.name: Combinatorial optimisation (annealing, QAOA)
families.idea: Encodes a discrete optimisation as an energy landscape (QUBO / Ising) and searches for low-energy solutions.
uses: Portfolio selection with cardinality or lot constraints
families.hardware: Quantum annealers, neutral atoms (analog mode), gate-based
families.status: Runs today on small and medium instances. No robust advantage over good MILP solvers or classical heuristics at scale. Theoretical scaling results for QAOA exist (JPMorgan, Argonne, Quantinuum, 2025) but are not yet a practical edge.
families.noRegret: Write the problem as a MILP or QUBO and benchmark commercial solvers, simulated annealing and GPU heuristics. A clean formulation is needed whatever the hardware.

families.name: Quantum machine learning (kernels, variational models)
families.idea: Maps data into a quantum state space and trains a classifier or regressor there.
families.status: Most hyped, least proven. No reproducible advantage on real financial data against strong classical baselines; several proposed speed-ups have been dequantised. HSBC and IBM reported better bond-trade fill predictions in 2025, as a preliminary, not independently replicated result.
families.noRegret: Strong classical baselines (gradient boosting, well-tuned neural nets), feature engineering, and an ML validation framework (explainability, stability, drift).

families.name: Quantum generative models (Born machines, quantum GANs)
families.idea: Uses the output distribution of a quantum circuit as a generative model, which can represent some distributions compactly.
families.status: Research stage: a few dozen qubits, coarse distributions, few assets. No evidence yet of better tails or dependence than classical generators.
families.noRegret: Historical simulation, then GARCH and copulas, then classical generative models (VAE, GAN, diffusion), each with a documented validation of tails and stylised facts.

families.name: Linear systems and PDE solvers (HHL family)
families.idea: Solves large linear systems or PDEs with a cost that grows slowly with dimension, under strict conditions.
families.status: Speed-ups hold only when inputs load efficiently and a summary statistic is enough as output. For most finance PDEs these conditions remove the advantage.
families.noRegret: Efficient PDE schemes, sparse grids and tensor-train methods.

families.name: Quantum-inspired methods (tensor networks, digital annealers)
families.idea: Classical algorithms borrowed from quantum physics, run on CPUs and GPUs.
families.hardware: Classical CPU / GPU, or dedicated classical chips (Fujitsu Digital Annealer, Toshiba SQBM+)
families.status: Usable today. Banks report speed-ups and smaller memory footprints in pilots (for example Crédit Agricole CIB with Multiverse and Pasqal, NatWest with Fujitsu).
families.noRegret: Yes: this is itself a no-regret step, and it builds the skills quantum methods will need.

families.name: Certified randomness
families.idea: Uses a quantum computer to produce random numbers whose randomness can be verified.
families.status: Demonstrated by JPMorgan and Quantinuum (Nature, 2025). Niche: pseudo-random generators are fine for Monte Carlo pricing.
families.noRegret: Nothing to change in pricing; check random-number generator quality and seed management.

families.name: Shor's algorithm (cryptanalysis)
families.idea: Factors integers and computes discrete logarithms efficiently, which breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.
uses: A threat to encryption and signatures, not a tool
families.status: Estimates keep falling: under a million noisy qubits for RSA-2048 (Gidney, 2025). Data harvested today can be decrypted later. NIST published post-quantum standards in 2024.
families.noRegret: Post-quantum cryptography migration: inventory, crypto-agility, priority to long-lived data. Out of Veqctor's scope, but the one quantum topic that needs action now.

hardware.how: Circuits cooled near absolute zero act as artificial atoms.
hardware.strengths: Fast gates (nanoseconds), mature fabrication, widest cloud access and software ecosystem.
hardware.limits: Cryogenics and wiring at scale; mostly nearest-neighbour connectivity; many physical qubits per logical qubit.
hardware.state: IBM Nighthawk (120 qubits) and Loon test chip; Google Willow (105 qubits) showed error rates falling as codes grow (2024). IBM targets Starling, about 200 logical qubits, in 2029; Google targets useful error-corrected machines by the end of the decade.

hardware.how: Superconducting cavities encode qubits that suppress one type of error by design.
hardware.strengths: Fewer physical qubits per logical qubit in principle.
hardware.limits: Early: tens of qubits; full error correction not yet shown at scale.
hardware.state: Alice & Bob (16 cat qubits; on-premise system; 18-qubit system ordered by GENCI). AWS Ocelot chip (2025).

hardware.how: Charged atoms held by electric fields, manipulated with lasers.
hardware.strengths: Highest fidelities, all-to-all connectivity, best logical-qubit results today.
hardware.limits: Slow gates (microseconds to milliseconds), scaling traps to thousands of ions.
hardware.state: Quantinuum Helios (98 qubits, about 48 logical qubits; record 99.9995% logical-memory fidelity, October 2026). Sol planned 2027, Apollo (fault-tolerant) 2029. IonQ Tempo (64 algorithmic qubits) after buying Oxford Ionics.

hardware.how: Atoms held in optical tweezers, entangled through Rydberg states.
hardware.strengths: Scale (arrays of thousands of atoms), reconfigurable connectivity, analog mode suited to optimisation.
hardware.limits: Slower cycles, atom loss, two-qubit fidelity around 99.5%; error-corrected computation (not just memory) still to prove.
hardware.state: Dozens of logical qubits shown (QuEra/Harvard, Atom Computing/Microsoft, Infleqtion). Microsoft and Atom Computing building Magne (about 50 logical qubits). Google added a neutral-atom programme in March 2026. Pasqal systems run in European HPC centres.

hardware.how: Qubits carried by photons on chips, mostly at room temperature.
hardware.strengths: Standard chip fabrication, natural networking, modular scale-up.
hardware.limits: Photon loss and probabilistic gates; no large general-purpose machine yet.
hardware.state: PsiQuantum building utility-scale sites in Brisbane and Chicago (late 2020s target). Xanadu Aurora (modular, 35 chips). Quandela in DARPA's benchmarking initiative.

hardware.how: Electron spins in silicon, made with chip-industry processes.
hardware.strengths: CMOS manufacturing and very high qubit density in principle.
hardware.limits: Small systems so far; two-qubit fidelity around 99%.
hardware.state: Quobly (€115m raised, first product targeted end 2026), Quantum Motion system at the UK NQCC, Diraq, Intel. C12 works on carbon nanotubes.

hardware.how: Qubits stored in exotic quasi-particles (Majorana modes), protected from noise by physics.
hardware.strengths: Very low error rates in theory, small footprint.
hardware.limits: The existence of a working topological qubit is still disputed by physicists.
hardware.state: Microsoft Majorana 1 (2025) and Majorana 2 (June 2026) prototypes, a few qubits.

hardware.how: Special-purpose superconducting machines that relax to low-energy solutions of an optimisation problem.
hardware.strengths: Thousands of qubits available today for optimisation and sampling.
hardware.limits: Not universal; advantage over classical heuristics contested.
hardware.state: D-Wave Advantage2 (4,400+ qubits). D-Wave also bought Quantum Circuits (2026) to add gate-based machines.

hardware.how: Classical hardware running algorithms borrowed from quantum physics.
hardware.limits: No quantum speed-up; gains are classical algorithmic ones.
hardware.state: Tensor-network software and dedicated chips (Fujitsu Digital Annealer, Toshiba SQBM+) used in bank pilots.
